lead: After the FM discriminator, noise power grows with audio frequency, so the treble sounds hissy. Pre-emphasis boosts the treble in the transmitter before modulation; de-emphasis cuts it by the same amount in the receiver after detection. The programme comes back flat, but the high-frequency noise is cut on the way. Broadcast FM uses a 50 µs time constant in most of the world and 75 µs in the Americas and South Korea. The same trick is used in TV sound, wireless microphones and analogue tape.
prereq: You need: the parabolic noise spectrum of FM (see Noise in AM and FM receivers).

blocks.text: The noise at the receiver input is white. The discriminator turns a frequency offset into a voltage, so a noise component f hertz from the carrier gives an output voltage proportional to f, and a power proportional to f². Across the audio band the noise power density rises as a parabola; the amplitude rises as a straight line, the noise triangle.

Speech and music have most of their energy at low and middle frequencies; high notes and consonants are weaker. So the treble has the least signal exactly where the noise is greatest, and the treble SNR is poor even when the overall SNR looks good.

Pre-emphasis fixes this before transmission. The transmitter passes the audio through a network that boosts the high frequencies; the receiver passes the discriminator output through the inverse network. The programme is boosted and then cut back, so it ends where it started. The noise is added in between, so it is only cut. One condition: the boost raises the peak audio voltage and hence the deviation, so the deviation limit must be set after the pre-emphasis network.

sections.h3: The two responses and the improvement

blocks.text: The pre-emphasis network is a first-order boost set by a time constant τ = RC.
f is the audio frequency in Hz; f<sub>1</sub> the corner frequency in Hz; τ in seconds. Below f<sub>1</sub> the gain is about 1; above it the gain rises at 6 dB per octave.
the same f<sub>1</sub> at both ends, so the two responses multiply to 1 at every frequency.
A practical pre-emphasis network (R1 in parallel with C, then a shunt R2) has a second corner well above the audio band, so the boost stops rising there. The table gives the two standards.

blocks.text: With de-emphasis, the output noise is the parabola f² weighted by 1/(1 + (f/f<sub>1</sub>)²). Integrating both over 0 to W and dividing gives the improvement in output SNR (the deviation is reset so the signal power is unchanged):

W is the highest audio frequency in Hz; arctan in radians; I is a power ratio. For W much larger than f<sub>1</sub> it tends to (1/3)(W/f<sub>1</sub>)², which underestimates I by 1 to 1.5 dB at broadcast values.

Put pre-emphasis in the audio path before the FM modulator, and de-emphasis after the discriminator, before the audio amplifier. The transmitter network must see the microphone or line signal, not the modulated carrier; the receiver network must see the recovered audio, not the IF.

The time constants must match. With a 75 µs transmitter and a 50 µs receiver, the treble is cut too little, so the sound is bright and hissy. With a 50 µs transmitter and a 75 µs receiver, the treble is cut too much and the sound is dull.

In a stereo receiver de-emphasis goes after the stereo decoder, on the recovered left and right signals (or on L + R and L − R after detection). It must not act on the composite baseband, where the L − R signal sits at 23 to 53 kHz and would be cut almost flat, and the 19 kHz pilot would be weakened (see FM stereo multiplexing).

examples.question: A broadcast FM system uses 75 µs pre-emphasis and a 15 kHz audio band. Find the corner frequency, the boost at the corner and at 15 kHz, and the SNR improvement from the exact formula and from the large-W approximation.
examples.answer: f<sub>1</sub> = 2122 Hz; boost 3.01 dB at f<sub>1</sub> and 17.07 dB at 15 kHz; improvement 20.88 (13.2 dB), against 16.65 (12.2 dB) from the approximation.

examples.question: Repeat for the 50 µs standard with W = 15 kHz, and compare with 75 µs.
steps: Approximation: 4.712²/3 = 7.40 = 8.69 dB, 1.5 dB low, because W/f<sub>1</sub> is not much larger than 1.
75 µs gives 3.0 dB more improvement, but its larger treble boost pushes the deviation up more on bright music.
examples.answer: 50 µs: f<sub>1</sub> = 3183 Hz, boost 13.66 dB at 15 kHz, improvement 10.41 (10.2 dB); 75 µs improves 3.0 dB more.

traps: Swapping the networks puts the boost in the receiver. The programme still comes out flat, but the receiver now boosts the discriminator noise: for 75 µs and a 15 kHz band the noise power rises 31 times (14.9 dB) instead of falling.
A voltage gain in dB is 20 log, not 10 log; the improvement I is a power ratio, so use 10 log.
Convert microseconds to seconds in f<sub>1</sub> = 1/(2πτ), or the corner is off by 10⁶.
Pre-emphasis does not remove the noise triangle; it lets de-emphasis cut the noise without cutting the programme.
The approximation (1/3)(W/f<sub>1</sub>)² underestimates the improvement by 1 to 1.5 dB at broadcast values; use the exact formula when the question asks for an exact value.

quiz.q: What is pre-emphasis and where is it placed?
quiz.a: A treble boost with time constant τ (corner 1/2πτ) in the audio path before the FM modulator.

quiz.q: Why does the discriminator output noise power rise as f²?
quiz.a: The discriminator turns frequency offset into voltage, so a noise component f hertz from the carrier gives a voltage proportional to f and a power proportional to f².

quiz.q: A 50 µs system is used. Find f<sub>1</sub> and the pre-emphasis gain at 10 kHz in dB.
Find the exact de-emphasis improvement for 75 µs and W = 15 kHz in dB.
Why must de-emphasis follow the discriminator, not precede it?
quiz.a: Before the discriminator the noise has not yet been shaped into a triangle, and an audio network on the IF would be meaningless. After it, the network cuts exactly the treble noise the discriminator made.

quiz.q: Why does pre-emphasis raise the FM deviation, and what is done about it?
quiz.a: The treble boost raises the peak audio voltage, so the peak frequency swing rises. The audio level (or a limiter) is set after the pre-emphasis network so the peak deviation stays within 75 kHz.

quiz.q: What is the product of the pre-emphasis and de-emphasis responses?
quiz.a: 1 at every frequency, so the programme comes out flat.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software FM receivers apply de-emphasis as a one-pole IIR filter after the discriminator. Broadcasters add audio processors that limit the boosted treble so the deviation stays legal. Similar emphasis curves appear in analogue tape, vinyl (RIAA) and early CD pre-emphasis. Search for FM pre-emphasis 50 µs 75 µs and RIAA equalisation.
